The gap in wage gains between people who switched jobs and those who stayed in their jobs is now closing.
On average, people who changed jobs have almost always gotten better pay raises than those who stayed, but in the past the difference was usually around one percentage point.
But now wage growth is slowing down for everyone, and job switchers are getting smaller wage bumps in their new jobs.

The labor market is likely cooling, because even a shortage of workers isn't overcoming the historic imbalance between employers and employees in the US: the volume of income that workers take home as a proportion of what the US economy produces is still falling.

The new study looked at how men and women were dividing work at home and why they divided it that way.
In general, both men and women took more responsibility for tasks they liked.
For example, men liked yard care and home maintenance more than women.
They leaned toward wanting primary responsibility for such tasks.
The researchers added that there was not a single childcare task that men liked more than women.
Keep in mind, however, that as with any research on group differences, there were large within-group differences.
The authors noted that previous research revealed gender differences in attitudes towards family and career.

These differences appear as early as six years old: girls that age already show more interest in helping and caring for others than boys do, and they already exhibit a greater orientation toward family versus career.
